title: Building a Transformer from Scratch: Part 1 — The Embedding Layer
author: Dhruv
summary: Before the attention mechanism computes a single dot product in an autoregressive Transformer like GPT, the model faces a fundamental problem: neural networks do not understand text, and feeding them raw token IDs introduces false mathematical assumptions. If the tokenizer maps "cat" to index 200 and "dog" to 201 , a linear layer treats "dog" as having a higher numerical value than "cat" . Token IDs are discrete categorical variables, not ordinal measurements. The embedding layer bridges this gap. It maps discrete integers into continuous vector spaces where semantic relationships and sequence ordering can actually be learned. Here is how the embedding layer works under the hood, along with a production-grade PyTorch implementation. The Two Problems Embeddings Must Solve 1. Semantic Representation (Token Embeddings) A tokenizer splits raw text into tokens and assigns each one an integer ID. To eliminate arbitrary numerical ordering, we map each ID to a learned vector of dimension d_model via a token lookup matrix W_e of shape (vocab_size, d_model) . Through backpropagation, tokens that appear in similar linguistic contexts gravitate toward each other in this high-dimensional vector space. 2. Sequence Order (Positional Embeddings) Unlike Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which process tokens step-by-step from left to right, Transformers process the entire sequence in parallel. Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant, the model would process "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" identically without an explicit position signal. To fix this, we map each sequence position 0, 1, ..., seq_len - 1 to a positional embedding vector of dimension d_model . PyTorch Implementation This module combines token embeddings with learned absolute positional embeddings and dropout regularization, matching the architectural setup used in GPT-2. python import torch import torch.nn as nn class TransformerEmbeddings(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, d_model: int, max_seq_len: int, dropout: float = 0.1): super().__init__() self.d_model = d_model # Token lookup matrix: shape (vocab_size, d_model) self.token_embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model) # Position lookup matrix: shape (max_seq_len, d_model) self.position_embeddings = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model) # Regularization: applies dropout across the summed embeddings self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout) def forward(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Expected input shape: (batch_size, seq_len) batch_size, seq_len = input_ids.shape # Guard clause: prevent context window overflows if seq_len > self.position_embeddings.num_embeddings: raise ValueError( f"Sequence length ({seq_len}) exceeds maximum context window " f"({self.position_embeddings.num_embeddings})" ) # Generate positional indices [0, 1, ..., seq_len - 1] # Shape: (1, seq_len), created directly on the input's target device positions = torch.arange(0, seq_len, device=input_ids.device).unsqueeze(0) # Retrieve vectors tok_emb = self.token_embeddings(input_ids) # (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) pos_emb = self.position_embeddings(positions) # (1, seq_len, d_model) # Combine via broadcasting: (batch_size, seq_len, d_model) embeddings = tok_emb + pos_emb return self.dropout(embeddings) # Sanity check execution block if __name__ == "__main__": vocab_size, d_model, max_len = 50257, 768, 1024 layer = TransformerEmbeddings(vocab_size, d_model, max_len, dropout=0.1) # Dummy batch of 2 sequences, each 8 tokens long dummy_input = torch.randint(0, vocab_size, (2, 8)) output = layer(dummy_input) print(f"Input shape: {dummy_input.shape}") # torch.Size([2, 8]) print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}") # torch.Size([2, 8, 768]) assert output.shape == (2, 8, d_model), "Shape mismatch!" print("Embedding module ran successfully.")

title: Google Jobs results as JSON, for $1 per 1,000 jobs (no proxies, no browser)
author: eden
summary: Google Jobs is the best free job index on the web. It pulls listings from LinkedIn, Indeed, company career sites and hundreds of smaller boards into one search. What it does not have is an API. The scrapers that fill that gap tend to break: they drive a browser through Google, get blocked, and you pay for failed runs. In October 2026 the most used one on the Apify Store failed 19% of its runs and charged $0.35 to $0.90 per 100 jobs, and another succeeded in only 1 of 500 runs in a month. So I built one that does not scrape Google from a browser at all. It reads Google Jobs through a commercial search-data API, so there are no proxies to rotate and nothing to break. This post shows how to use it. What you get per job You send one or more searches and a country, optionally a city. You get one record per job: { "query" : "data engineer" , "country" : "US" , "position" : 1 , "title" : "Senior Data Engineer" , "company" : "Acme Corp" , "location" : "Austin, TX" , "contract_type" : "Full-time" , "salary" : "$140K–$180K a year" , "salary_min" : 140000 , "salary_max" : 180000 , "salary_currency" : "USD" , "salary_period" : "year" , "posted_ago" : "2 days ago" , "source" : "LinkedIn" , "apply_url" : "https://..." } (Example of the output format.) What to expect from real data: in a test of 3 US searches (30 jobs), Google showed a salary on 5 of the 30 jobs. Many apply links go straight to the company's own career site. The full job description text is not included; the apply_url leads to it. Run it The tool is the Google Jobs Scraper Actor on Apify. From the console Open the Actor, type your searches, pick a country, optionally a city such as Austin,Texas , and press Start. Results appear as a table you can export to CSV, Excel or JSON. Pricing $0.005 per search that returns jobs. Searches with no results are free. $0.001 per job. 100 jobs from one search cost about $0.11. You need an Apify account. You can try it on the free Apify plan: each free run returns the first 10 jobs of your first search. Full results need a paid Apify plan , because every search has a real data cost. title: Building a Production-Ready FastMCP Server Integration for Cognee Knowledge Graphs
author: FOKRUL ISLAM
summary: Overview Context fragmentation is one of the most critical bottlenecks when building autonomous AI agents. While LLMs excel at localized reasoning, they lose track of structured graph relationships across multi-turn sessions and disjointed tool calls. To solve this, I built a production-ready FastMCP (Model Context Protocol) server integration for Cognee , allowing standard MCP clients (such as Claude Desktop and Cursor) to read from and write to persistent knowledge graphs seamlessly. Architecture & Integration Flow The integration lives under cognee/api/mcp/ and bridges standard MCP client requests directly into Cognee's engine. text +------------------------------------+ | Claude Desktop / Cursor / Agent | +------------------------------------+ | (MCP Protocol via stdio) v +------------------------------------+ | FastMCP Server (server.py) | +------------------------------------+ | | v v [cognee_add_memory] [cognee_search_memory] | | +---------> <---------+ | v Cognee Knowledge Graph & FalkorDB Exposed Core Tools The server implements two deterministic async tools: cognee_add_memory: Ingests raw text or structured document payloads into Cognee's ingestion pipeline, automatically cognifying and extracting entity relationships into the graph. cognee_search_memory: Executes hybrid vector and graph queries across the knowledge graph to retrieve grounded context for reasoning. Implementation Snippet (server.py) Python from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP import cognee mcp = FastMCP("Cognee-Context-Engine") @mcp.tool() async def cognee_add_memory(content: str, dataset_name: str = "main") -> str: """Ingest context into Cognee knowledge graph.""" await cognee.add(content, dataset_name=dataset_name) await cognee.cognify(dataset_name=dataset_name) return "Memory successfully cognified." @mcp.tool() async def cognee_search_memory(query: str) -> str: """Retrieve grounded context from the knowledge graph.""" results = await cognee.search(query_text=query) return str(results) if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run(transport="stdio") Claude Desktop Configuration To connect this integration with Claude Desktop, add the server to your claude_desktop_config.json: JSON { "mcpServers": { "cognee": { "command": "python", "args": ["-m", "cognee.api.mcp.server", "--transport", "stdio"], "env": { "OPENAI_API_KEY": "your-api-key" } } } } Testing & Verification The integration includes a full mock test suite using pytest covering: Correct tool schema dispatching. Graceful handling of empty queries and malformed payloads. Case insensitivity and dataset segregation. Result: 10/10 unit tests passed (100% green) in 0.06 seconds. Hackathon Submission This integration is submitted for Mergetober / Graph Hacks under Cognee Pull Request #5864.

title: Is that really a Dogecoin address? Checking D... vs 0x... before anyone loses coins
author: Bardo Lindqvist
summary: I nearly lost 500 DOGE to a dropdown. A casino cashier listed Dogecoin twice, once as the native coin and once as a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain, and the BEP-20 option came first. I copied the address it gave me, pasted it into my wallet and only then saw the 0x at the start. I stopped before sending. Plenty of people don't. I spent eight years testing payment flows, and this one's a classic edge case: two things with the same name and different rails. If you build anything that takes or sends DOGE, the cheapest fix is to check the address format before a single coin moves. Here's how, with nothing but the Python standard library. Two families of "DOGE" addresses Starts with What it is Format D Native Dogecoin, pay-to-public-key-hash Base58Check, version byte 0x1E , 34 characters 9 or A Native Dogecoin, pay-to-script-hash Base58Check, version byte 0x16 0x An EVM address (BNB Smart Chain, Ethereum…), where a token borrows the DOGE ticker 0x + 40 hex characters A native Dogecoin wallet won't send to a 0x address, and coins sent the other way land on a chain the receiving service may never look at. The first character tells you which world you're in, but the first character alone isn't validation: typos and truncated pastes start with D too. Base58Check in a few lines A native address is 25 bytes encoded in Base58: one version byte, a 20-byte hash, and a 4-byte checksum, which is the first four bytes of a double SHA-256 of the first 21. Decode, split, recompute, compare. import hashlib import re ALPHABET = " 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz " DOGE_VERSIONS = { 0x1E : " P2PKH " , 0x16 : " P2SH " } # mainnet: D... and 9.../A... EVM_RE = re . compile ( r " ^0x[0-9a-fA-F]{40}$ " ) def b58decode ( s : str ) -> bytes : n = 0 for ch in s : i = ALPHABET . find ( ch ) if i < 0 : raise ValueError ( f " not base58: { ch !r} " ) n = n * 58 + i raw = n . to_bytes (( n . bit_length () + 7 ) // 8 , " big " ) pad = len ( s ) - len ( s . lstrip ( " 1 " )) return b " \x00 " * pad + raw def classify ( address : str ) -> str : address = address . strip () if EVM_RE . match ( address ): return " evm " # BEP-20 / ERC-20 style: not a Dogecoin address try : data = b58decode ( address ) except ValueError : return " invalid " if len ( data ) != 25 : return " invalid " payload , checksum = data [: - 4 ], data [ - 4 :] if hashlib . sha256 ( hashlib . sha256 ( payload ). digest ()). digest ()[: 4 ] != checksum : return " invalid " kind = DOGE_VERSIONS . get ( payload [ 0 ]) return f " doge- { kind . lower () } " if kind else " invalid " classify returns one of four answers: doge-p2pkh , doge-p2sh , evm or invalid . A Bitcoin legacy address passes the checksum but has version byte 0x00 , so it comes back invalid , which is what you'd want in a DOGE field. What to test The edge cases I'd put in any test suite for this field: a real D… address, and the same address with one character changed (checksum must fail) a 9… or A… script address 0x followed by 40 hex characters (must be flagged, not rejected silently) a Bitcoin address, a Litecoin address, an empty string, a string with spaces around it the characters Base58 leaves out on purpose: 0 , O , I , l What to do with the answer Validation is half the job. The other half is what the person at the screen sees: evm in a DOGE field: say so in words. "This is a BNB Smart Chain address, not a Dogecoin one" saves more coins than a red border. Two networks for one ticker: default to the native chain, label the other one with its chain name, not just "DOGE". No memo field for native DOGE. If your form shows one for Dogecoin, people will assume something's wrong. They'll be right. Show the first and last characters back after paste, so people compare what they meant with what they copied. None of this needs a node or an API call. It runs before the request leaves the page, and that's where a payment bug costs the least, give or take a support ticket. I test crypto casino cashiers the way I used to test checkouts. The write-ups are at dogecasino.best, and the raw numbers are on GitHub .

title: How to turn Google Maps Scraper output into a scored local SEO lead list
author: Alex Rowan
summary: By Alex Rowan Disclosure: Manta Media, the local SEO agency I work at, built the two Apify Actors linked near the end of this post (Google Maps Leads Scorer and Local SEO Bulk Site Auditor). Every step here also works in your own script, and the code is included. A Google Maps scrape gives you a long list of businesses: names, phones, websites, ratings. What it doesn't tell you is which of them actually need help with their website or local SEO. If you do outreach for an agency or as a freelancer, emailing all 200 is a waste of everyone's time. This walkthrough goes from a raw Maps scrape to a short, ranked list with one concrete talking point per business. You can do every step yourself in Python, or use an Actor for the scoring part. Step 1: Scrape one niche in one city Run Google Maps Scraper ( compass/crawler-google-places ) for a single category and location. Keep it to one location per run, as the Actor's own input form recommends. { "searchStringsArray" : [ "plumber" ], "locationQuery" : "Beaverton, OR, USA" , "maxCrawledPlacesPerSearch" : 50 , "language" : "en" } Each place in the output dataset includes, among many other fields, title , website , phone , totalScore (rating), reviewsCount , categoryName and city . Those seven fields are all we need. Note the run's dataset ID ; you'll pass it to the next step. Step 2: Decide what "needs help" means These are the checks we use per business. Each one is cheap: one fetch of the homepage, plus robots.txt and an http:// redirect check. No website at all. The clearest lead for a web designer. No LocalBusiness structured data. No JSON-LD telling Google the business name, address and phone. Title and meta description. A missing meta description, or a title over ~60 characters that gets cut off in results. Phone and address on the homepage. Local visitors expect to see them, and Google reads them too. HTTPS. A valid certificate, and http:// redirecting to https:// . Reviews vs the local median. 3 reviews means little on its own. Against a group median of 31 (from the sample run below), it's a concrete talking point. Checking for LocalBusiness JSON-LD takes only a few lines of Python: import json , requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup LOCAL = { " LocalBusiness " , " Plumber " , " Dentist " , " HVACBusiness " , " RoofingContractor " } # extend as needed def local_schema ( url ): html = requests . get ( url , timeout = ( 10 , 20 ), headers = { " User-Agent " : " my-audit-bot/1.0 " }). text soup = BeautifulSoup ( html , " lxml " ) for tag in soup . find_all ( " script " , type = " application/ld+json " ): try : data = json . loads ( tag . string or "" ) except ValueError : continue for d in ( data if isinstance ( data , list ) else data . get ( " @graph " , [ data ])): t = d . get ( " @type " , []) if set ( t if isinstance ( t , list ) else [ t ]) & LOCAL : return { " type " : t , " name " : d . get ( " name " ), " telephone " : d . get ( " telephone " )} return None Compare the schema telephone with the phone shown on the page. A mismatch is a real NAP (name, address, phone) problem worth pointing out. Step 3: Score and tier Add the signals into one 0-100 opportunity score , where higher means a better prospect. These are the weights the Google Maps Leads Scorer documents in its README: Signal Points SEO gap: 100 minus the site's local SEO score, scaled up to 35 No LocalBusiness schema +10 No SSL (or no https redirect) +8 (+4) No meta description / no title +5 / +4 No mobile viewport +5 No phone on the homepage / no street address (on the page or in schema) +4 / +3 Slow site (over 3 s to respond, or PageSpeed mobile under 50 when enabled) +5 Reviews below the batch median (scaled by how far below) up to +15 Rating under 4.0 (under 4.5) +7 (+3) Public contact email found (only when findEmails is on) +10 No website 85 base Website failed to load 45 base Review and rating points are added on top of the base for no-website and site-down leads too. Scores are capped at 100. Tiers: hot is ≥ 50 or no website, warm is ≥ 30, cold is < 30. Tune the weights to whatever you sell. A web designer might weight "no website" and "no viewport" higher; an SEO agency might weight schema and reviews. Be polite You're visiting small-business websites, so keep the load trivial: Respect robots.txt, and skip pages it disallows. Use low concurrency (we use 3) and conservative timeouts (10 s connect / 20 s read). Cap the download size per page, and use an identifiable User-Agent. Run each site with a hard time limit. One pathological page shouldn't stall the whole batch. Only collect emails a business shows publicly on its own site, and follow CAN-SPAM / GDPR / PDPA when you contact anyone. Results from a real run Here are real rows from a published sample run of the Scorer on Beaverton, OR plumbers (scored 12 Oct 2026, email search off). You can open the full output yourself: JSON · CSV . Business Reviews Local SEO score Opportunity Tier Precision Plumbing Beaverton 3 51 48 warm Anctil Plumbing Inc 31 68 27 cold Leak Locaters 185 82 10 cold Two things stand out. The business with the fewest reviews and the weakest site comes out on top, which is the point of scoring. And a high review count doesn't mean a well-optimised site: in a larger run, Apollo Plumbing, Heating, AC & Electric had 2,014 reviews but a local SEO score of 20 and no LocalBusiness schema, which put it in the hot tier. That's why it's worth scoring the website rather than filtering on reviews alone. The practical outcome: instead of emailing every place on the scrape, you start with the hot and warm rows and one specific, checkable observation for each. Doing it without writing the code Disclosure again: Manta Media built both of these Actors. We packaged this workflow as Google Maps Leads Scorer ($0.008 per scored lead; leads that time out are not charged). Paste the Google Maps Scraper dataset ID into datasetId : { "datasetId" : "<your Google Maps Scraper dataset ID>" , "maxLeads" : 200 , "findEmails" : true } You get one row per business with opportunityScore , tier , pitchPoints , email , localSeoScore , reviewMedian and seoIssues . The Google Maps fields title , website , phone , totalScore , reviewsCount , categoryName and city are mapped automatically. Sort by opportunityScore and start with the hot tier. If you only need the website checks for a list of URLs, the sister Actor Local SEO Bulk Site Auditor does that for $0.004 per URL. Either way, the steps above work just as well in your own script. What matters is the order: scrape, check, score, then contact only the top of the list. If you want the whole setup I use around this (the agent instructions, site templates and pre-send checks), it is in the Lead Site Crew Kit , $39.

title: 124 "Dofollow" Directories, Fact-Checked: 39 Pass Nothing
author: Céline
summary: My SaaS, Awiser, had a low Domain Rating. Every growth thread says the same thing: submit to directories, collect dofollow links, watch your DR climb. Before spending a dollar, I wanted to know which of those lists were telling the truth. So I took 124 directories, launch sites and dev platforms from those lists and had AI agents read every pricing, submit and FAQ page. Then I checked them against five published audits of real listings' HTML, all from September and October 2026. Where no audit covers a site, I quote its own page. 39 of them pass nothing to a new listing. You get a nofollow or ugc link, a redirect, or no link at all. Product Hunt is on that list. So are G2, Capterra and Indie Hackers. Below are the 39 to skip, the 11 free ones with no strings and the 13 that cost $15 or less. Then a 10-second DevTools check, so you can test any list yourself. This one included. TL;DR 124 checked. 52 can give you a dofollow link. 39 give a new listing nothing. 29 more I couldn't verify, and 4 are press platforms where a journalist decides. Only 11 directories give a free dofollow link with no badge, no fee and no top-3 lottery. The best of them, SaaSHub (DR 80), only follows your link once you verify the listing. Most of the 52 that work want something. 29 want money. 9 want a badge on your site. "Free dofollow" usually comes with fine print: a top-3 ranking, an upvote threshold, a badge you can never remove, or a queue of up to 60 weeks. 13 directories promise a dofollow link in writing for $15 or less. Don't trust any list, this one included. The snippet below checks a live listing in 10 seconds. What "dofollow" actually means There is no rel="dofollow" . A link is followed when its rel attribute is empty, or holds only browser flags like noopener and noreferrer . Three values switch it off. rel value Meant for Followed? empty, noopener , noreferrer Normal links Yes nofollow Links the site doesn't vouch for No ugc Comments, forum posts, user profiles No sponsored Ads and paid placements No Google says links marked nofollow , ugc or sponsored "will generally not be followed" . Ahrefs is blunter: only followed links increase DR , and only the first one from each domain. A clean rel can still hide a dead link: A redirect. The button points to the directory's own short link, which forwards to you. If that hop is nofollow or noindex , like Dang.ai's, nothing reaches you. A plain 301 may pass value, but no page check can prove it. A JavaScript button. No <a href> , nothing for a crawler to follow. A page-level block. A noindex listing page drops out of Google, which eventually stops following its links . A nofollow robots meta tag switches off every link on the page at once. The 39 that pass nothing These show up on almost every "best dofollow directories" list. Here is what a new listing on each one actually gets you, as checked in September and October 2026. Two can pay off later: Hacker News follows a story from about 12 points, and AlternativeTo follows some established apps. Paid listings get a nofollow redirect Product Hunt 91 rel="ugc" on all 20 product pages checked, and 11 of 20 launch-day pages were noindex Hacker News 91 nofollow on every story under 9 points, a plain link from about 12 G2 91 No link at all on free profiles. Paid ones go through a nofollow click tracker Capterra 91 No link on free profiles. The paid button has no href Crunchbase 91 nofollow Awwwards 89 nofollow , after a $65 submission fee Wellfound 87 nofollow F6S 83 nofollow Dang.ai 82 Its free plan requires a crawlable link to dang.ai. Visitors come back through a redirect served as noindex, nofollow Indie Hackers 82 rel="nofollow noopener" AlternativeTo 81 nofollow on new listings Peerlist 77 Only the weekly top 5 get a link, and it's ugc Futurepedia 73 nofollow tool links Writing platforms don't save you either. Links inside Medium articles and GitHub READMEs are nofollow ( checked in July ), and Hashnode and HackerNoon mark article links nofollow or ugc ( checked in September ). The other 20 include review sites that show no link at all, like GetApp, Software Advice and SoftwareSuggest. Others are closed: I found no public way to add a new tool to StackShare, CodeProject is archived, and Gartner Peer Insights only lists enterprise software. All 39 are in the full table linked at the end. The fine print behind "free dofollow" Most directories that do give a followed link attach a condition. It sits in their pricing table, not on the list that sent you there. I found five patterns. Win your day. Open-Launch, Startup Fast and Aura++ share one pricing template: "Dofollow Backlink only if" you finish in the top 3 of the day and display their badge. LaunchIgniter and LaunchVault run the same rule weekly. For a new product with no audience, that means nofollow . Hit a score. On Uneed , a free launch needs an upvote score of 20 for the dofollow link, or 10 with the $14.99 Fast-track. Of 60 launches from October 3 to 5 , 48 were followed. All 12 nofollow ones sat at 8 points or less. Pay. DevHunt's FAQ says it plainly: free listings are nofollow , paid launches get a permanent dofollow link. 90 of 92 free pages checked were nofollow . All 97 paid pages were followed. Show their badge, forever. Startup Fame, Fazier, Twelve Tools, Turbo0 and ToolPilot give a real dofollow link for free if you link back. ToolFame and SaaSFame unpublish you when the badge comes off. That's a link exchange, and Google's spam policies list excessive link exchanges as link spam. Wait. OpenHunts' free queue is about 60 weeks. SaaSFame reviews free listings "within 180 days". Huzzler's free page waits 72 days and ships noindex . The rules also move under you. Uneed's free line closed on August 17 and reopened on September 11 with new rules. BetaList now charges for every submission , and its Visit Site button goes through a plain 301 redirect, which SaaSCity counts as followed. The 11 directories that give a free dofollow link, no strings No badge, no fee, no ranking contest. Some make you wait, and one makes you verify.
